blocks.text: It is said that electric current is the flow of charge. In a conductor the charge carriers are the free electrons. When the ends of a conductor are connected to a battery or some other source, an electric field is set up at every point within the conductor. The free electrons experience a force in the direction of -E and start moving. As they bump among the atoms they are not accelerated in a straight line; they keep colliding with the atoms of the conductor. The overall effect of these collisions is to transfer the energy of the accelerated electrons to the lattice, with the result that the electrons acquire an average velocity, called the drift velocity, in the direction of -E. The drift velocity is of the order of 10^-3 m s^-1, and this drift of electrons forms the electric current.

The slow drift velocity does not mean that it takes a long time for a current to set up; as soon as we switch on a bulb it lights up immediately. On turning the switch on, all the free electrons in the circuit start drifting together: they repel the neighbouring ones and the disturbance propagates along the wire almost instantaneously. That is why the current is set up very rapidly.

blocks.title: Electric current
blocks.text: If a net charge Q passes through any cross-section of a conductor in time t, the current through it is I = Q/t ... (9.28). The SI unit of current is the ampere (A): the current due to the flow of one coulomb of charge per second.

If the charges move around a circuit in the same direction at all times, the current is direct current (D.C.); batteries produce direct current. If the charges move first one way and then the opposite way, changing direction at regular intervals, the current is alternating current (A.C.); mostly electric generators produce A.C., and the electricity supplied to our homes, offices and factories by power stations is A.C.

The electric current in metal wires is due to the flow of electrons, but early scientists believed that it was due to the flow of positive charges. Scientists have kept the convention and take the direction of current flow to be the direction in which positive charges would move; we call it conventional current.

blocks.title: Conventional current
blocks.text: Conventional current is the hypothetical flow of positive charges that would have the same effect in the circuit as the flow of negative charges that actually does occur.

In Fig. 9.20 negative electrons arrive at the positive terminal of the battery; the same effect would be achieved if an equivalent amount of positive charge left the positive terminal. Therefore the conventional current flows from the positive terminal towards the negative terminal through the external circuit. Conventional current is consistent with our earlier use of a positive test charge for defining electric fields and potential: its direction is always from a point of higher potential towards a point of lower potential. From now on the current I always means the conventional current.

blocks.prompt: If the drift velocity is only about 10^-3 m s^-1, why does a bulb light as soon as it is switched on?
blocks.explanation: The wire is already full of free electrons. Closing the switch sets up the electric field along the whole circuit almost at once, so all the free electrons, including those in the bulb's filament, start drifting together; no electron has to travel from the switch to the bulb.

items: Free electrons drift against E with drift velocity about 10^-3 m s^-1, colliding with the lattice; the field spreads at once, so current starts immediately. I = Q/t (9.28); 1 A = 1 C s^-1. D.C. one way (batteries); A.C. reverses (generators, mains).
Conventional current: the equivalent flow of positive charge, from higher to lower potential (+ to - outside the source), opposite to electron flow.
